what_it_does: Memory deduplication is a technique where the operating system scans all the pages of RAM (4 KB chunks of memory) across all running programs and, when it finds identical copies, merges them into a single shared copy to save space — a feature called KSM (Kernel Same-page Merging) in Linux. A separate performance optimization called huge pages lets the OS group 512 consecutive 4 KB pages into one large 2 MB page, which makes memory lookups faster because the processor's address-translation cache (called the TLB, a small lookup table that converts logical addresses to physical ones) can cover more memory with fewer entries. The conflict is that deduplication breaks up these large pages, and the TLB miss penalty from falling back to 4 KB pages can degrade performance by up to 43%. Gemina solves this by separately tracking which pages are duplicate (eligible for deduplication) and which are hot (accessed frequently, so they benefit from being large pages), and by reorganizing memory so that frequently accessed pages can be quickly promoted back into large pages even after deduplication has fragmented them.
